disease_info: Adjustment Disorder involves the development of emotional or behavioral symptoms in response to an identifiable stressor, occurring within months of the event and causing marked distress or functional impairment beyond what would be expected. Clinically, it often presents with mood changes, anxiety, or maladaptive behaviors tied closely in time and content to specific life events such as relationship conflict, health changes, or occupational stress. The course is typically time-limited, with symptoms resolving within six months after the stressor or its consequences end, though it can persist if the stressor is ongoing. It is distinguished from normal stress reactions by the degree of impairment and from other disorders (e.g., major depression, PTSD) by its less severe, more situationally bound presentation and the absence of defining features such as full depressive episodes or trauma-related re-experiencing.

narrative.stressor: About six months ago, Thomas had to shut down his small handyman side business after losing a major contracting opportunity due to licensing and insurance paperwork he had procrastinated, which also led to a dispute with a long-time client over unfinished work. Around the same time, his chronic back pain worsened, making it harder to take on heavier jobs and pushing him fully out of the workforce just as his family was counting on his income to cover rising living costs and his daughter’s community college tuition. Over the next five months, he found himself increasingly stuck between guilt over not contributing financially and avoidance of the administrative steps needed to restart in a more formal way, spending more time alone on the river or in his workshop but leaving projects half-organized and ignoring calls from former customers. His wife finally pressed him to see a mental health professional after he began backing out of club activities and community volunteer commitments, telling her he felt like he no longer knew how to respond to the pressure of getting his work life back on track.
narrative.chief_complaint: I feel like I’ve shut down and keep reacting badly ever since my work fell apart, and I can’t seem to handle anything that reminds me of getting back into business.

narrative.stressor: Five months ago, Maria’s school district implemented a sudden restructuring that reassigned her from her long-standing bilingual classroom to a larger, mixed-ability class with a rigid scripted curriculum, while also cutting the arts-integrated and social-emotional programs she had helped build. At the same time, new evaluation metrics tied to standardized test scores placed intense pressure on veteran teachers like her, and several close colleagues either retired early or transferred, leaving her feeling isolated and undermined in the work that had anchored her identity for decades. Over the following months, she brought more grading and planning home, stopped enjoying her watercolor sessions and salsa nights, and began dreading each school day, noticing that her usual optimism and mentoring energy had been replaced by a sense that she was constantly failing her students under the new system. After her principal gently noted a decline in her classroom engagement and she caught herself snapping at a student for a minor behavior issue—something very out of character—she agreed to her sister’s suggestion to seek psychiatric help because she felt her reactions to the changes at work were overwhelming her and spilling into every part of her life.
narrative.chief_complaint: Ever since they changed everything at school, I feel like I’m not handling it well at all and my reactions to the stress are taking over my life.

narrative.stressor: Roughly five months ago, Gabriel’s wife was diagnosed with early-stage dementia after a series of memory lapses and confused episodes, and he suddenly found himself coordinating her medical appointments, managing her medications, and taking on most of the household tasks she used to handle. At the same time, his employer reduced his hours due to a warehouse automation initiative, which disrupted his long-standing routine and left him torn between relief at having more time to care for her and worry about their future stability. Over the ensuing months, he began declining invitations from his walking club and church volunteer group, spending more time at home monitoring her and second-guessing every decision about her care, while feeling increasingly unsettled about how quickly his orderly life had changed. After his adult daughter visited and noticed how preoccupied and tense he had become about even minor changes in his wife’s condition, she encouraged him to talk to a mental health professional so he could find a healthier way to respond to all the new responsibilities and uncertainty.
narrative.chief_complaint: Since my wife’s dementia diagnosis, I feel like I’m not coping well with all the changes and I’m reacting to every little thing like it’s a crisis.
